source.text: בַּיָּמִ֣ים הָהֵ֔ם חָלָ֥ה חִזְקִיָּ֖הוּ לָמ֑וּת וַיָּבֹ֣א אֵ֠לָיו יְשַׁעְיָ֨הוּ בֶן־אָמ֜וֹץ הַנָּבִ֗יא וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אֵלָ֜יו כֹּֽה־אָמַ֤ר יְהוָה֙ צַ֣ו לְבֵיתֶ֔ךָ כִּ֛י מֵ֥ת אַתָּ֖ה וְלֹ֥א תִֽחְיֶֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: In the days those became sick Hezekiah to die, and came to him Isaiah son of Amoz the prophet and said to him, thus says Yahweh: command to your household, for dying you [are] and not you will live.

en.L: In those days Hezekiah became sick to [the point of] dying, and Isaiah son of Amoz, the prophet, came to him and said to him, "Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: Give command to your household, for you are dying, and you will not live."
en.B: In those days Hezekiah fell ill and was close to death. The prophet Isaiah son of Amoz came to him and said, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} says this: Give final instructions to your household, for you are dying and will not live."
en.R: Around that time Hezekiah became so sick that he was about to die. The prophet Isaiah son of Amoz came to see him. He said, "This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says: Tell your family what they must do after you are gone. You are going to die. You will not get well."

decisions.choice: in those days: during the years of Sennacherib's threat to Jerusalem
decisions.reason: The phrase ties the illness loosely to the events of chapters 18-19. Verse 6 still promises rescue from the king of Assyria, so the illness came before that danger had ended. 2 Chronicles 32:24 tells the same event briefly.

decisions.choice: give command to your household: settle your affairs and give your last instructions before death
decisions.reason: The same words are said to Ahithophel before he dies (2 Samuel 17:23). A dying man told his family how his goods and duties were to be handled.

decisions.choice: you are dying, and you will not live: death is near and the illness will not be cured
decisions.reason: The participle describes death as already on its way. The second clause says the same thing again from the other side: Hezekiah will not recover. Verse 5 shows that the sentence could still be turned back in answer to prayer.

decisions.choice: the same account as Isaiah 38:1-8 and 39:1-8
decisions.reason: Verses 1-19 of this chapter tell the same story as Isaiah 38-39, often in the same words. This verse is word for word the same as Isaiah 38:1, and is rendered the same way. Where the two accounts differ, a note on that verse says how. The poem Hezekiah wrote after his recovery (Isaiah 38:9-20) has no parallel in Kings.

decisions.choice: Tell your family what they must do after you are gone
decisions.reason: Readable spells out what the idiom means (m2), as at Isaiah 38:1.

source.text: וַיַּסֵּ֥ב אֶת־פָּנָ֖יו אֶל־הַקִּ֑יר וַיִּ֨תְפַּלֵּ֔ל אֶל־יְהוָ֖ה לֵאמֹֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: And he turned his face to the wall and prayed to Yahweh, saying:

en.L: And he turned his face to the wall and prayed to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, saying,
en.B: Hezekiah turned his face toward the wall and prayed to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}:
en.R: Hezekiah turned over to face the wall, and he prayed to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}:

decisions.choice: turned his face to the wall: turned away from the people in the room to pray alone
decisions.reason: Lying on his sickbed, the king turns away from those around him. The act shows that his prayer is private and earnest, not that he turns from God (compare 1 Kings 21:4, where Ahab turns his face away in sulking).

decisions.choice: the same as Isaiah 38:2, without the name and with "saying"
decisions.reason: Isaiah 38:2 names Hezekiah as the one who turned. Kings says only "he" and ends with "saying", which leads straight into the prayer; Isaiah begins the prayer with "and he said" instead (Isaiah 38:3).

decisions.choice: Hezekiah
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the king, who is the subject from verse 1, as Isaiah 38:2 does.

source.text: אָנָּ֣ה יְהוָ֗ה זְכָר־נָ֞א אֵ֣ת אֲשֶׁ֧ר הִתְהַלַּ֣כְתִּי לְפָנֶ֗יךָ בֶּֽאֱמֶת֙ וּבְלֵבָ֣ב שָׁלֵ֔ם וְהַטּ֥וֹב בְּעֵינֶ֖יךָ עָשִׂ֑יתִי וַיֵּ֥בְךְּ חִזְקִיָּ֖הוּ בְּכִ֥י גָדֽוֹל׃ס

records.literal_gloss: Please, Yahweh, remember please how I have walked before you in faithfulness and with a heart whole, and the good in your eyes I have done. And wept Hezekiah weeping great.

en.L: "Please, {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, remember, please, how I have walked before {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} in faithfulness and with a whole heart, and [that] I have done what [is] good in {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} eyes." And Hezekiah wept [with] great weeping.
en.B: "Please, {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, remember how I have lived before {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} faithfully and with an undivided heart, doing what is good in {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} sight." And Hezekiah wept loudly.
en.R: "{{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, please remember how I have always been faithful to {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}. I have served {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} with all my heart. I have done what {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} see as good." Then Hezekiah cried very hard.

decisions.choice: walked before you: lived my whole life in your presence and service
decisions.reason: To walk before God is to live in his sight and serve him (Genesis 17:1; 1 Kings 2:4). Hezekiah does not claim to be sinless (Isaiah 38:17 speaks of his sins); he appeals to a life of loyalty, the life described in 18:3-6.

decisions.choice: in faithfulness and with a whole heart: with steady loyalty and undivided devotion
decisions.reason: A whole (complete) heart is one not split between God and other loyalties (1 Kings 8:61; 11:4). The word for faithfulness comes back in verse 19, where it is paired with peace.

decisions.choice: word for word the same prayer as Isaiah 38:3
decisions.reason: The prayer and the note of Hezekiah's weeping are the same as in Isaiah 38:3, and are rendered the same way. Only the opening differs: Isaiah begins "And he said", where Kings has "saying" at the end of verse 2.

decisions.choice: I have always been faithful to you. I have served you with all my heart.
decisions.reason: Readable breaks the prayer into short sentences and explains the idiom of walking before God (m1), as at Isaiah 38:3.

source.text: וַיְהִ֣י יְשַׁעְיָ֔הוּ לֹ֣א יָצָ֔א חָצֵ֖ר הַתִּֽיכֹנָ֑ה וּדְבַר־יְהוָ֔ה הָיָ֥ה אֵלָ֖יו לֵאמֹֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was, Isaiah not had gone out [of the] court the middle, and [the] word of Yahweh came to him, saying:

en.L: And it happened [that] Isaiah had not [yet] gone out [of] the middle court, and the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} came to him, saying,
en.B: Isaiah had not yet left the middle courtyard when the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} came to him:
en.R: Before Isaiah had even left the middle courtyard of the palace, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} gave him a message:

decisions.choice: the middle court: the reading given in the margin
decisions.reason: The consonants written in the text spell "the city", which gives "the middle city", an odd phrase for a place inside Jerusalem. The Hebrew margin tells the reader to read "court" instead, and the ancient Greek translation also has "the middle court". The margin's reading is followed. On either reading Isaiah had hardly left the palace grounds.

decisions.choice: the middle court: one of the courtyards of the royal buildings
decisions.reason: The king's palace stood next to the temple, with courtyards around and between the buildings (1 Kings 7:1-12). Isaiah had just left Hezekiah's sickroom and was still crossing one of these courts when the new word came. The answer to the prayer came at once.

decisions.choice: Isaiah 38:4 does not say where Isaiah was
decisions.reason: Isaiah 38:4 has only "And the word of the LORD came to Isaiah, saying". Kings adds that Isaiah had not yet gone out of the middle court, and says the word came "to him".

decisions.choice: yet
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says he "had not gone out"; "yet" makes clear that he was still on his way out. Literal brackets it. Readable says the same with "before ... even".

source.text: שׁ֣וּב וְאָמַרְתָּ֞ אֶל־חִזְקִיָּ֣הוּ נְגִיד־עַמִּ֗י כֹּֽה־אָמַ֤ר יְהוָה֙ אֱלֹהֵי֙ דָּוִ֣ד אָבִ֔יךָ שָׁמַ֨עְתִּי֙ אֶת־תְּפִלָּתֶ֔ךָ רָאִ֖יתִי אֶת־דִּמְעָתֶ֑ךָ הִנְנִי֙ רֹ֣פֶא לָ֔ךְ בַּיּוֹם֙ הַשְּׁלִישִׁ֔י תַּעֲלֶ֖ה בֵּ֥ית יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: Turn back and you will say to Hezekiah [the] ruler of my people, thus says Yahweh the God of David your father: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears; here I [am] healing you; on the day the third you will go up [to the] house of Yahweh.

en.L: "Go back and say to Hezekiah, the ruler of {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} people, 'Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of David your father: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Look, I am healing you. On the third day you will go up [to the] house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.B: "Go back and say to Hezekiah, the ruler of {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} people, '{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of your ancestor David, says this: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. I am about to heal you, and on the third day you will go up to the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.R: "Go back and tell Hezekiah, the leader of {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} people, 'This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says, the God your ancestor David served: I have heard your prayer, and I have seen you crying. So I will heal you. On the third day you will be well enough to go up to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}'s house.

decisions.choice: the ruler of my people: the one God has set over his people
decisions.reason: The title is the one given to Saul and David when God chose them (1 Samuel 9:16; 2 Samuel 7:8). It reminds Hezekiah that he holds the kingdom from God and rules God's people, not his own.

decisions.choice: David your father: David your ancestor
decisions.reason: David lived about three hundred years before Hezekiah. Calling God the God of David reminds Hezekiah of the promise made to David's line (2 Samuel 7:16), which verse 6 goes on to name.

decisions.choice: here I am healing you: the healing is as good as done
decisions.reason: The particle with a participle announces what God is about to do. The same verb comes back in Hezekiah's question in verse 8.

decisions.choice: on the third day you will go up to the house of the LORD: in two days he would be well enough to worship at the temple
decisions.reason: Days were counted with the present day as the first, so the third day is the day after tomorrow. To go up to the temple was to appear in public again and give thanks there (compare Isaiah 38:20). The promise names a near and checkable day, which is why Hezekiah asks for a sign in verse 8.

decisions.choice: differs from Isaiah 38:5 in three places
decisions.reason: Isaiah 38:5 has "Go" where Kings has "Go back", does not have "the ruler of my people", and does not have "I am healing you; on the third day you will go up to the house of the LORD". In Isaiah 38:5 the speech goes straight on to the fifteen years. Isaiah keeps only Hezekiah's question about going up to the house of the LORD (Isaiah 38:22).

decisions.choice: leader
decisions.reason: Readable says "leader" for the title "ruler", as throughout these books.

decisions.choice: you will be well enough to go up
decisions.reason: Readable says why going up to the temple matters: it would mean he was healed (m4).

source.text: וְהֹסַפְתִּ֣י עַל־יָמֶ֗יךָ חֲמֵ֤שׁ עֶשְׂרֵה֙ שָׁנָ֔ה וּמִכַּ֤ף מֶֽלֶךְ־אַשּׁוּר֙ אַצִּ֣ילְךָ֔ וְאֵ֖ת הָעִ֣יר הַזֹּ֑את וְגַנּוֹתִי֙ עַל־הָעִ֣יר הַזֹּ֔את לְמַֽעֲנִ֔י וּלְמַ֖עַן דָּוִ֥ד עַבְדִּֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: And I will add to your days fifteen year[s], and from [the] palm of [the] king of Assyria I will deliver you and the city this, and I will defend over the city this for my sake and for the sake of David my servant.

en.L: And I will add fifteen years to your days, and from the hand of the king of Assyria I will deliver you and this city, and I will defend this city for {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} sake and for the sake of David {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} slave.'"
en.B: I will add fifteen years to your days. I will rescue you and this city from the grasp of the king of Assyria, and I will shield this city for {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} own sake and for {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} servant David's sake.'"
en.R: I will let you live fifteen more years. I will save you and this city from the power of the king of Assyria. I will protect this city for {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} own honor, and because of the promise I made to {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} servant David.'"

decisions.choice: I will add fifteen years: a promise of a set span of life
decisions.reason: The fifteen years fit the history: Hezekiah's illness came about 701 BC, and his reign ended about 686 BC. His son Manasseh was twelve when he became king (21:1), so he was born in these added years.

decisions.choice: from the palm of the king: from his power and control
decisions.reason: Hand or palm stands for the power to hold and harm (18:29-35).

decisions.choice: I will defend this city for my sake and for David's: the promise already given in 19:34
decisions.reason: God made the same promise, in the same words, in 19:34 (Isaiah 37:35). Isaiah 38:6 repeats only "I will defend this city"; Kings repeats the whole promise. Isaiah 38:5 also says "Look, I am adding" where Kings says "And I will add"; the sense is the same.

decisions.choice: for my sake and for the sake of David: God acts for his own name and his promise to David
decisions.reason: The Assyrian king had mocked the LORD as one more god who could not save (18:33-35; 19:10-13). God defends the city to show who he is, and to keep his promise that David's line would rule in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 7:16; 1 Kings 11:13).

decisions.choice: slave
decisions.reason: Literal says "slave" in "my servant David", as throughout these books; Balanced and Readable say "servant". Isaiah 38:6 does not have these words. At 19:34 every level keeps "servant", because that verse repeats Isaiah 37:35.

decisions.choice: for my own honor, and because of the promise I made to my servant David
decisions.reason: Readable says what acting for God's own sake and for David's sake means (m4), as at Isaiah 37:35.

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יְשַֽׁעְיָ֔הוּ קְח֖וּ דְּבֶ֣לֶת תְּאֵנִ֑ים וַיִּקְח֛וּ וַיָּשִׂ֥ימוּ עַֽל־הַשְּׁחִ֖ין וַיֶּֽחִי׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Isaiah, take a cake of figs. And they took and they put [it] on the boil, and he lived.

en.L: And Isaiah said, "Take a cake of figs." And they took [it] and laid [it] on the boil, and he lived.
en.B: Then Isaiah said, "Bring a lump of pressed figs." They brought it and spread it on the sore, and he recovered.
en.R: Then Isaiah said, "Bring some pressed figs." They brought them and put them on Hezekiah's sore, and he got well.

decisions.choice: a cake of figs on the boil: a common remedy
decisions.reason: Pressed figs were made into cakes for food (1 Samuel 25:18) and were also used to dress sores. The illness is named as a boil or inflamed sore, the word used of the boils in Exodus 9:9. God gives the healing; the figs are the means.

decisions.choice: the figs are applied here; Isaiah 38:21 places the order at the end
decisions.reason: In Isaiah 38:21 the order comes after Hezekiah's poem, as a look back: "let them take a cake of figs and rub it on the boil, and he will live". Kings tells it here, in the flow of the story, and says it was done: they took the figs and laid them on the boil, and he lived.

decisions.choice: and he lived: he recovered, the outcome told ahead of the sign
decisions.reason: Verse 7 ends the healing story with its outcome. Verse 8 then goes back to Hezekiah's question, asked before the third day came, and verses 9-11 tell the sign. The order is by topic, not strictly by time.

decisions.choice: Hezekiah's sore
decisions.reason: Readable names whose sore it was.

source.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ אֶֽל־יְשַׁעְיָ֔הוּ מָ֣ה א֔וֹת כִּֽי־יִרְפָּ֥א יְהוָ֖ה לִ֑י וְעָלִ֛יתִי בַּיּ֥וֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁ֖י בֵּ֥ית יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Hezekiah to Isaiah, what [is the] sign that will heal Yahweh me, and I will go up on the day the third [to the] house of Yahweh?

en.L: And Hezekiah said to Isaiah, "What [is the] sign that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will heal me, and [that] I will go up on the third day [to the] house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}?"
en.B: Hezekiah had asked Isaiah, "What sign will there be that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is going to heal me, and that on the third day I will go up to the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}?"
en.R: Hezekiah had asked Isaiah, "What sign will show me that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will heal me? How will I know that I will go up to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}'s house on the third day?"

decisions.choice: the sign: a visible event that guarantees the promise
decisions.reason: A sign is something God does that can be seen, given to confirm a word that has not yet come true (19:29; Isaiah 7:11, 14). Hezekiah asks for one; his father Ahaz had refused the sign God offered him (Isaiah 7:10-12).

decisions.choice: Hezekiah asked: the question came before the healing described in verse 7
decisions.reason: The verb is the usual one for the next step in a story, but the question belongs before the third day, when the healing was still to come (see verse 7, m3). The question looks back to the promise of verse 5.

decisions.choice: a fuller form of the question in Isaiah 38:22
decisions.reason: Isaiah 38:22 asks only "What is the sign that I will go up to the house of the LORD?" and puts the question at the end of the chapter. Kings adds "that the LORD will heal me" and "on the third day", and puts the question before the sign is given.

decisions.choice: had asked
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use "had asked" so the question does not seem to come after the recovery told in verse 7 (m2), as Isaiah 38:22 does.

decisions.choice: two questions
decisions.reason: Readable splits the one Hebrew question into two shorter ones.

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יְשַׁעְיָ֗הוּ זֶה־לְּךָ֤ הָאוֹת֙ מֵאֵ֣ת יְהוָ֔ה כִּ֚י יַעֲשֶׂ֣ה יְהוָ֔ה אֶת־הַדָּבָ֖ר אֲשֶׁ֣ר דִּבֵּ֑ר הָלַ֤ךְ הַצֵּל֙ עֶ֣שֶׂר מַֽעֲל֔וֹת אִם־יָשׁ֖וּב עֶ֥שֶׂר מַעֲלֽוֹת׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Isaiah, this [is] for you the sign from Yahweh, that will do Yahweh the thing which he has spoken: has gone the shadow ten steps, or will it go back ten steps?

en.L: And Isaiah said, "This [is] the sign for you from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will do the thing that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has spoken: [shall] the shadow go forward ten steps, or shall it go back ten steps?"
en.B: Isaiah answered, "This will be your sign from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will carry out what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has said: Should the shadow go forward ten steps, or should it go back ten steps?"
en.R: Isaiah answered, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} will give you a sign to show that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will do what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has promised. You choose: Should the shadow move ahead ten steps, or should it go back ten steps?"

decisions.choice: shall the shadow go forward ten steps, or go back: Hezekiah is offered a choice
alternatives: The shadow has gone forward ten steps; shall it go back ten steps?
decisions.reason: The first verb is in a form that normally speaks of the past and has no question marker, so the line could be read "The shadow has gone forward ten steps; shall it go back ten steps?" But the word "or" sets two options side by side, and Hezekiah's answer in verse 10 chooses between them. The record reads the whole line as a question offering a choice.

decisions.choice: Isaiah 38:7-8 has no choice
decisions.reason: In Isaiah 38:7-8 God simply announces that the shadow will go back ten steps. In Kings Isaiah lets Hezekiah choose which way the shadow will move. The opening words are almost the same as Isaiah 38:7, which has "this thing" where Kings has "the thing".

decisions.choice: the shadow and the steps: the shadow moving on a stairway as the day passes
decisions.reason: As the sun moved across the sky, the shadow cast on a stairway crept along the steps and marked the time of day (verse 11). To go forward is to move the way it always moves; to go back is to move against the course of the day.

decisions.choice: shall; should; You choose
decisions.reason: Literal brackets "shall" to show the question that the line implies (m1). Readable adds "You choose" to make plain that Hezekiah is being offered a choice.

source.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ יְחִזְקִיָּ֔הוּ נָקֵ֣ל לַצֵּ֔ל לִנְט֖וֹת עֶ֣שֶׂר מַעֲל֑וֹת לֹ֣א כִ֔י יָשׁ֥וּב הַצֵּ֛ל אֲחֹרַנִּ֖ית עֶ֥שֶׂר מַעֲלֽוֹת׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Hezekiah, [it is] trifling for the shadow to stretch out ten steps; no, but let go back the shadow backward ten steps.

en.L: And Hezekiah said, "It is a light thing for the shadow to stretch out ten steps. No, rather let the shadow go back backward ten steps."
en.B: Hezekiah answered, "It is easy for the shadow to lengthen ten steps. No, let the shadow go back ten steps."
en.R: Hezekiah answered, "It is easy for the shadow to move ahead ten steps, because that is what it always does. No, make the shadow go back ten steps."

decisions.choice: it is a light thing for the shadow to stretch out: going forward would be no real sign
decisions.reason: To stretch out is to lengthen, the way a shadow moves on as the day goes on. That would happen anyway, so it would prove nothing. A shadow moving back, against the course of the day, could only be God's doing.

decisions.choice: Hezekiah: here spelled in a longer form of the name
decisions.reason: Hebrew spells the king's name in more than one way. This verse uses a longer form, Yehizkiyahu, built on the verb form "he strengthens"; both forms mean "Yah strengthens". It is the same man.

decisions.choice: because that is what it always does
decisions.reason: Readable says why going forward would be easy (m1).

decisions.choice: Hezekiah
decisions.reason: Every level keeps the usual form of the name, since the longer spelling names the same king.

source.text: וַיִּקְרָ֛א יְשַׁעְיָ֥הוּ הַנָּבִ֖יא אֶל־יְהוָ֑ה וַיָּ֣שֶׁב אֶת־הַצֵּ֗ל בַּֽ֠מַּעֲלוֹת אֲשֶׁ֨ר יָרְדָ֜ה בְּמַעֲל֥וֹת אָחָ֛ז אֲחֹֽרַנִּ֖ית עֶ֥שֶׂר מַעֲלֽוֹת׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And called Isaiah the prophet to Yahweh, and he brought back the shadow on the steps which it had gone down on [the] steps of Ahaz, backward ten steps.

en.L: And Isaiah the prophet called out to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} brought the shadow back on the steps, which it had gone down on the steps of Ahaz, backward ten steps.
en.B: Then the prophet Isaiah called out to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} made the shadow go back ten steps, back up the steps of Ahaz that it had gone down.
en.R: Then the prophet Isaiah called out to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} made the shadow go back up ten of the steps it had already gone down on the stairway of Ahaz.

decisions.choice: the steps of Ahaz: a stairway built by Ahaz, on which the moving shadow showed the time of day
decisions.reason: The word means steps or stairs. As the sun moved, a shadow crept down the stairs, marking the hours. Some take the steps as the markings of a sundial; either way the shadow moved backward, against the course of the day. Ahaz was Hezekiah's father (16:20).

decisions.choice: the LORD brought the shadow back after Isaiah called out to him
decisions.reason: Isaiah 38:8 gives God's words announcing the sign and then says "the sun went back ten steps". Kings says that Isaiah called out to the LORD and that the LORD brought the shadow back. Both speak of "the steps of Ahaz".

decisions.choice: which it had gone down: the shadow, moved by the sun
decisions.reason: The verb "had gone down" has a feminine form, which fits the word for the sun better than the word for the shadow. Isaiah 38:8 names the sun here ("gone down on the steps of Ahaz with the sun"). The sense is the same: the shadow had moved down the steps as the sun moved, and now it went back.

decisions.choice: the LORD
decisions.reason: Readable names the LORD as the one who brought the shadow back, since a new sentence begins.

source.text: בָּעֵ֣ת הַהִ֡יא שָׁלַ֡ח בְּרֹאדַ֣ךְ בַּ֠לְאֲדָן בֶּֽן־בַּלְאֲדָ֧ן מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶ֛ל סְפָרִ֥ים וּמִנְחָ֖ה אֶל־חִזְקִיָּ֑הוּ כִּ֣י שָׁמַ֔ע כִּ֥י חָלָ֖ה חִזְקִיָּֽהוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: At the time that sent Berodach-baladan son of Baladan king of Babylon letters and a gift to Hezekiah, for he had heard that had been sick Hezekiah.

en.L: At that time Berodach-baladan son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a gift to Hezekiah, for he had heard that Hezekiah had been sick.
en.B: About that time Berodach-baladan son of Baladan, the king of Babylon, sent letters and a present to Hezekiah, because he had heard that Hezekiah had been ill.
en.R: At about that time, the king of Babylon heard that Hezekiah had been sick. The king's name was Berodach-baladan son of Baladan. He sent Hezekiah letters and a gift.

decisions.choice: the king of Babylon: Marduk-apla-iddina II, a Chaldean ruler who fought Assyria for control of Babylon
decisions.reason: He ruled Babylon from 722 to 710 BC and again briefly in 703 BC, and twice led revolts against Assyria. His embassy to Hezekiah fits that history: he was looking for allies in the west against Assyria.

decisions.choice: Berodach-baladan: the same king Isaiah 39:1 calls Merodach-baladan
decisions.reason: Kings spells the name with a B where Isaiah 39:1 has an M. Merodach is the Hebrew form of Marduk, the chief god of Babylon, so the M spelling is closer to the king's own name; the two sounds are close, and the B form may be a copying slip or another way of saying it. The record keeps the spelling each book has.

decisions.choice: a shorter reason than Isaiah 39:1
decisions.reason: Isaiah 39:1 says the king of Babylon "heard that he had been sick and had become strong". Kings says only that he had heard "that Hezekiah had been sick", and names Hezekiah again. 2 Chronicles 32:31 adds that the envoys came to ask about the sign done in the land, and that God left Hezekiah to test him.

decisions.choice: the king of Babylon heard ... He sent Hezekiah letters and a gift.
decisions.reason: Readable puts the cause first and gives the king's name in a sentence of its own, as at Isaiah 39:1.

source.text: וַיִּשְׁמַ֣ע עֲלֵיהֶם֮ חִזְקִיָּהוּ֒ וַיַּרְאֵ֣ם אֶת־כָּל־בֵּ֣ית נְכֹתֹ֡האֶת־הַכֶּסֶף֩ וְאֶת־הַזָּהָ֨ב וְאֶת־הַבְּשָׂמִ֜ים וְאֵ֣ת׀שֶׁ֣מֶן הַטּ֗וֹב וְאֵת֙ בֵּ֣ית כֵּלָ֔יו וְאֵ֛ת כָּל־אֲשֶׁ֥ר נִמְצָ֖א בְּאֽוֹצְרֹתָ֑יו לֹֽא־הָיָ֣ה דָבָ֗ר אֲ֠שֶׁר לֹֽא־הֶרְאָ֧ם חִזְקִיָּ֛הוּ בְּבֵית֖וֹ וּבְכָל־מֶמְשַׁלְתּֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: And listened to them Hezekiah, and he showed them all [the] house of his treasure, the silver and the gold and the spices and the oil the good, and [the] house of his weapons, and all that was found in his storehouses; not was a thing that not showed them Hezekiah in his house and in all his realm.

en.L: And Hezekiah listened to them, and he showed them all his treasure house, the silver and the gold and the spices and the good oil, and his armory, and all that was found in his storehouses. There was not a thing in his house and in all his realm that Hezekiah did not show them.
en.B: Hezekiah listened to them and showed them his whole treasury: the silver and the gold, the spices and the fine oil, his armory, and everything to be found in his storehouses. In his palace and across his whole kingdom, there was nothing he did not let them see.
en.R: Hezekiah listened to the messengers. He showed them all the silver and gold, the spices, and the expensive olive oil in his treasure house. He showed them his weapons and everything else in his storerooms. He let them see everything in his palace and in his whole kingdom.

decisions.choice: listened to them: gave the envoys a hearing
decisions.reason: Isaiah 39:2 has a verb that differs by one letter in Hebrew: Hezekiah "rejoiced over them". Kings has "listened to them", that is, he heard their message with favor. Both readings show a king pleased to be courted by a foreign power.

decisions.choice: his treasure house and his armory: the wealth and the military strength of the kingdom
decisions.reason: Showing a foreign envoy one's treasure and weapons was a way of proving one's worth as an ally. The treasury had been emptied to pay Sennacherib (18:15-16), so this display may belong to the years after the Assyrian crisis or be part of it; the text does not say.

decisions.choice: the good oil: fine olive oil, a costly product kept in royal stores
decisions.reason: Fine oil was a valued trade good and was stored with spices and precious metals (2 Chronicles 32:27-28).

decisions.choice: otherwise the same as Isaiah 39:2, with "all" in a different place
decisions.reason: Kings says Hezekiah showed them "all his treasure house" and "his armory"; Isaiah 39:2 has "his treasure house" and "all his armory". The rest of the verse is the same and is rendered the same way.

decisions.choice: palace
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "palace" for the king's house; Literal keeps "house".

source.text: וַיָּבֹא֙ יְשַֽׁעְיָ֣הוּ הַנָּבִ֔יא אֶל־הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ חִזְקִיָּ֑הוּ וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אֵלָ֜יו מָ֥ה אָמְר֣וּ׀הָאֲנָשִׁ֣ים הָאֵ֗לֶּה וּמֵאַ֨יִן֙ יָבֹ֣אוּ אֵלֶ֔יךָ וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ חִזְקִיָּ֔הוּ מֵאֶ֧רֶץ רְחוֹקָ֛ה בָּ֖אוּ מִבָּבֶֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: And came Isaiah the prophet to the king Hezekiah and said to him, what did they say the men these, and from where do they come to you? And said Hezekiah, from a land distant they have come, from Babylon.

en.L: And Isaiah the prophet came to King Hezekiah and said to him, "What did these men say, and from where do they come to you?" And Hezekiah said, "From a distant land they have come, from Babylon."
en.B: Then the prophet Isaiah came to King Hezekiah and asked him, "What did these men say? And where did they come from to visit you?" Hezekiah answered, "They came from a faraway country, from Babylon."
en.R: Then the prophet Isaiah went to King Hezekiah. He asked, "What did these men say? Where did they come from?" Hezekiah answered, "They came from a country far away. They came from Babylon."

decisions.choice: a distant land: Babylon, far to the east beyond the desert
decisions.reason: Hezekiah answers only the second question and says nothing of what the envoys said. The phrase "from a distant land" echoes what the Gibeonites claimed in Joshua 9:6-9 when they sought a treaty with Israel.

decisions.choice: the same as Isaiah 39:3 except "to me"
decisions.reason: Isaiah 39:3 has Hezekiah say "they have come to me"; Kings has "they have come". Otherwise the verse is the same and is rendered the same way.

source.text: וַיֹּ֕אמֶר מָ֥ה רָא֖וּ בְּבֵיתֶ֑ךָ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר חִזְקִיָּ֗הוּ אֵ֣ת כָּל־אֲשֶׁ֤ר בְּבֵיתִי֙ רָא֔וּ לֹא־הָיָ֥ה דָבָ֛ר אֲשֶׁ֥ר לֹֽא־הִרְאִיתִ֖ם בְּאֹצְרֹתָֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: And he said, what did they see in your house? And said Hezekiah, all that [is] in my house they saw; not was a thing that not I showed them in my storehouses.

en.L: And he said, "What did they see in your house?" And Hezekiah said, "All that [is] in my house they saw; there was not a thing in my storehouses that I did not show them."
en.B: He asked, "What did they see in your palace?" Hezekiah replied, "They saw all that is in my palace. In my storerooms there is not a thing I failed to show them."
en.R: Isaiah asked, "What did they see in your palace?" Hezekiah said, "They saw everything in my palace. I showed them everything in my storerooms."

decisions.choice: they saw everything: Hezekiah's answer repeats the narrator's words in verse 13
decisions.reason: Hezekiah answers openly, using almost the same words the narrator used. The repetition sets up the word of judgment that follows: all that they saw will be carried away (verse 17).

decisions.choice: word for word the same as Isaiah 39:4
decisions.reason: The Hebrew of this verse is the same as Isaiah 39:4, and it is rendered the same way.

decisions.choice: Isaiah asked
decisions.reason: Readable names the speaker.

source.text: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר יְשַׁעְיָ֖הוּ אֶל־חִזְקִיָּ֑הוּ שְׁמַ֖ע דְּבַר־יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Isaiah to Hezekiah, hear [the] word of Yahweh:

en.L: And Isaiah said to Hezekiah, "Hear the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}:
en.B: Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, "Listen to the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}:
en.R: Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, "Listen to this message from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}:

decisions.choice: the word of the LORD: Isaiah 39:5 has the fuller title
decisions.reason: Isaiah 39:5 has "the word of the LORD of hosts". Kings has the shorter "the word of the LORD". Otherwise the verse is the same as Isaiah 39:5 and is rendered the same way.

source.text: הִנֵּה֮ יָמִ֣ים בָּאִים֒ וְנִשָּׂ֣א׀כָּל־אֲשֶׁ֣ר בְּבֵיתֶ֗ךָ וַאֲשֶׁ֨ר אָצְר֧וּ אֲבֹתֶ֛יךָ עַד־הַיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּ֖ה בָּבֶ֑לָה לֹֽא־יִוָּתֵ֥ר דָּבָ֖ר אָמַ֥ר יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: Look, days [are] coming, and will be carried off all that [is] in your house and that have stored up your fathers until the day this, to Babylon; not will be left a thing, says Yahweh.

en.L: Look, days are coming when all that [is] in your house, and that your fathers have stored up until this day, will be carried off to Babylon; not a thing will be left, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.B: Look, a time is coming when all that is in your palace, everything your ancestors have laid up until today, will be hauled off to Babylon. Not one thing will remain, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.R: Someday everything in your palace will be taken away to Babylon. All the treasures your ancestors saved up until now will be taken. Nothing will be left. This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says.

decisions.choice: carried off to Babylon: the first word in Kings of exile to Babylon
decisions.reason: At this time Babylon was a small power looking to Judah for help against Assyria. The word looks ahead more than a century to Nebuchadnezzar, who carried off the treasures of the temple and the palace (24:13; 25:13-15).

decisions.choice: your fathers: your ancestors, the earlier kings of Judah
decisions.reason: The treasures had been stored up by the kings before Hezekiah. "Until this day" here is Hezekiah's own day, the time Isaiah is speaking.

decisions.choice: word for word the same as Isaiah 39:6
decisions.reason: The Hebrew of this verse is the same as Isaiah 39:6, and it is rendered the same way.

source.text: וּמִבָּנֶ֜יךָ אֲשֶׁ֨ר יֵצְא֧וּ מִמְּךָ֛ אֲשֶׁ֥ר תּוֹלִ֖יד יִקָּ֑חוּוְהָיוּ֙ סָֽרִיסִ֔ים בְּהֵיכַ֖ל מֶ֥לֶךְ בָּבֶֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: And some of your sons who will come forth from you, whom you will father, they will take, and they will be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.

en.L: And some of your sons who will come out from you, whom you will father, they will take, and they will be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon."
en.B: Some of your descendants, born of your own line, will be taken away, and they will serve as eunuchs in the palace of the Babylonian king."
en.R: Some of your own descendants will be taken away. They will be made eunuchs and will serve in the palace of the king of Babylon."

decisions.choice: your sons: your descendants, the royal family after you
decisions.reason: Sons often means descendants. The words "who will come from you, whom you will father" stress that it will be Hezekiah's own line. Daniel 1:3 tells of young men of the royal family taken to serve in the palace of Babylon.

decisions.choice: eunuchs: castrated servants at a foreign court
decisions.reason: The word can mean any high court official (it is used of Potiphar, a married man, in Genesis 39:1), but in a foreign king's palace, of captives taken from a royal family, it most likely means eunuchs, as at Isaiah 39:7 and 56:3-4.

decisions.choice: they will take: the reading given in the margin
decisions.reason: The consonants written in the text give "he will take"; the Hebrew margin reads "they will take", as Isaiah 39:7 has in its text. Either way the sense is that they will be taken away; the margin's reading is followed. Apart from this the verse is the same as Isaiah 39:7 and is rendered the same way.

decisions.choice: will be made eunuchs and will serve
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what being eunuchs in the palace means.

decisions.choice: eunuchs
decisions.reason: These books usually say "officials" for this word at Balanced and Readable. Here every level keeps "eunuchs", as Isaiah 39:7 does, because the sense is most likely the literal one (m2).

source.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ אֶֽל־יְשַֽׁעְיָ֔הוּ ט֥וֹב דְּבַר־יְהוָ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֣ר דִּבַּ֑רְתָּ וַיֹּ֕אמֶר הֲל֛וֹא אִם־שָׁל֥וֹם וֶאֱמֶ֖ת יִהְיֶ֥ה בְיָמָֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Hezekiah to Isaiah, good [is the] word of Yahweh which you have spoken. And he said, [is it] not, if peace and truth will be in my days?

en.L: And Hezekiah said to Isaiah, "Good [is] the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} that you have spoken." And he said, "[Is it] not [good], if there will be peace and stability in my days?"
en.B: Hezekiah answered Isaiah, "This word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} that you have brought is good." He was thinking, "Is it not good, if there will be peace and stability as long as I live?"
en.R: Hezekiah said to Isaiah, "This message from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} that you have given me is good." He said this because he thought, "Is that not good enough, if there will be peace and safety while I am alive?"

decisions.choice: is it not good, if: a question that expects the answer yes
alternatives: Why not, if there will be peace and stability in my days?
Is it not so? There will be peace and stability in my days.
decisions.reason: The words are short: "Is it not, if ...?" The question picks up the "good" of Hezekiah's first sentence: is it not good, if there will be peace in my days? It may also be read "Why not, if ...?" or "Is it not so? There will be peace in my days". All the readings give the same thought.

decisions.choice: and he said: he said to himself
decisions.reason: The second "he said" introduces Hezekiah's own reasoning, which may have been thought rather than spoken.

decisions.choice: good is the word: Hezekiah accepts the judgment
decisions.reason: He submits to God's word, as Eli did (1 Samuel 3:18). His relief that the disaster will not come in his own lifetime is told without comment; the reader is left to weigh it.

decisions.choice: peace and stability: safety and security
decisions.reason: The second word is the one that means faithfulness in verse 3. Paired with peace it means firmness or security: things will hold steady.

decisions.choice: Isaiah 39:8 has a statement where Kings has a question
decisions.reason: Isaiah 39:8 reads "For there will be peace and stability in my days". Kings asks "Is it not good, if there will be peace and stability in my days?" The first sentence is the same in both and is rendered the same way.

decisions.choice: He was thinking
decisions.reason: Balanced shows that the second "he said" is Hezekiah's inner thought (m2), as at Isaiah 39:8.

decisions.choice: He said this because he thought, "Is that not good enough
decisions.reason: Readable spells out the link between the two sayings (m1, m2).

source.text: וְיֶ֨תֶר דִּבְרֵ֤י חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ וְכָל־גְּב֣וּרָת֔וֹ וַאֲשֶׁ֣ר עָשָׂ֗ה אֶת־הַבְּרֵכָה֙ וְאֶת־הַתְּעָלָ֔ה וַיָּבֵ֥א אֶת־הַמַּ֖יִם הָעִ֑ירָה הֲלֹא־הֵ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים עַל־סֵ֛פֶר דִּבְרֵ֥י הַיָּמִ֖ים לְמַלְכֵ֥י יְהוּדָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And [the] rest of [the] matters of Hezekiah and all his might and how he made the pool and the conduit and brought the water to the city, [are] not they written on [the] book of [the] matters of the days of [the] kings of Judah?

en.L: And the rest of the matters of Hezekiah, and all his might, and how he made the pool and the conduit and brought the water into the city, are they not written in the book of the matters of the days of the kings of Judah?
en.B: The rest of the acts of Hezekiah, all his might, and the pool and the conduit he made to bring water into the city, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Judah.
en.R: Everything else Hezekiah did, his great deeds, and how he made the pool and the tunnel that brought water into the city, is written in the history of the kings of Judah.

decisions.choice: the book of the matters of the days of the kings of Judah: a royal record the writer could consult
decisions.reason: The sources formula, as at 1:18 and 8:23. The writer sends the reader to a fuller written record of Judah's kings, now lost. The question "are they not written ...?" means "they are written".

decisions.choice: his might: his strength and his mighty deeds
decisions.reason: The word means strength or valor, and in these formulas it covers a king's achievements, in war and in building (1 Kings 15:23).

decisions.choice: the pool and the conduit: Hezekiah's tunnel, which brought the water of the Gihon spring inside the city walls
decisions.reason: 2 Chronicles 32:30 says Hezekiah blocked the upper outlet of the waters of Gihon and channeled them down to the west side of the City of David. A long, winding tunnel cut through the rock from the Gihon spring to the pool of Siloam, at the southern end of the city, can still be walked today. An inscription in early Hebrew script found inside it tells how two teams of diggers, cutting from each end, met in the middle. Bringing the water inside the walls kept the city supplied during a siege and kept it from the enemy (2 Chronicles 32:2-4; Isaiah 22:9-11). The pool is most likely the pool at the tunnel's end.

decisions.choice: 2 Chronicles 32:32-33 closes Hezekiah's reign more fully
decisions.reason: Chronicles speaks of his good deeds, sends the reader to the vision of Isaiah and the book of the kings of Judah and Israel, and adds that he was buried in the upper part of the tombs of David's sons and honored by all Judah.

decisions.choice: a statement in place of the question
decisions.reason: As in the sources formula throughout these books, Balanced and Readable state as a fact what the Hebrew asks as a question; Literal keeps the question.

decisions.choice: his great deeds; the tunnel
decisions.reason: Readable says what "his might" refers to (m2) and calls the conduit a tunnel, which is what it was (m3).

source.text: וַיִּשְׁכַּ֥ב חִזְקִיָּ֖הוּ עִם־אֲבֹתָ֑יו וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ מְנַשֶּׁ֥ה בְנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And lay down Hezekiah with his fathers, and reigned Manasseh his son in his place.

en.L: And Hezekiah lay down with his fathers, and Manasseh his son reigned in his place.
en.B: Then Hezekiah rested with his ancestors, and his son Manasseh became king in his place.
en.R: Then Hezekiah died, and his son Manasseh became king after him.

decisions.choice: lay down with his fathers: died
decisions.reason: The death formula used for the kings throughout these books. Here no burial is named; 2 Chronicles 32:33 adds that he was buried in the upper part of the tombs of David's sons.

decisions.choice: Manasseh his son: the next king of Judah
decisions.reason: His reign is told in 21:1-18. He was twelve when he became king (21:1), so he was born during the fifteen years added to Hezekiah's life (verse 6).

decisions.choice: lay down with his fathers / rested with his ancestors / died
decisions.reason: The death formula's wording at each level, as throughout these books. Readable says only "died" because the Hebrew names no burial here.
